subtype: Happy for the friend chosen instead of self [Actor]
passage:
The sports room still had sugarcane pieces from the Pongal celebration stacked in one corner when Coach pinned up the district basketball squad. Shreya ran her finger down the list twice. Tanuja, Grade 10. No Shreya.
Behind her, Tanuja, her best friend since Class 3, squeaked. "Shreya. Shreya, I'm in!"
Shreya turned and hugged her hard, and the gladness was real; she had watched Tanuja practise free throws alone every evening since June. "You deserve it. Totally."
Later, in the empty changing room, Shreya sat on the bench with one shoe on and let her eyes sting for a minute. She had wanted it too. Then she wiped her face, tied the lace, and went to buy Tanuja a celebration rose milk.

qa.q: Since when had Tanuja practised free throws alone every evening?
qa.a: Since June.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling alone in the changing room?
qa.a: Shreya felt a quiet sadness at not being picked and let her eyes sting, even though her gladness for Tanuja was real.

qa.q: What would you say to Shreya about feeling both glad and sad?
qa.a: Both are real and allowed; taking a minute to feel the loss, as she did, can make the celebration with Tanuja sincere rather than forced.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel about Shreya's hug and the rose milk?
qa.a: Tanuja probably feels deeply supported and relieved that the selection has not come between the two best friends.

grounding: A teenager left off the squad is truly glad for the best friend who was picked, and sad for herself too.

subtype: Delight in a partner's or friend's joy [Actor]
passage:
Rongali Bihu was three days away, and Nikita had already bought the red-bordered gamosa she planned to give her boyfriend Bhupen at the Guwahati mela. Then his call came, crackly from his hostel terrace.
"Niki, the dance troupe picked me for the Delhi tour. We leave Friday. I'll miss the whole Bihu week."
Her phone was at four percent. She pressed it to her ear, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt. "You got it! You practised that dhol step for months!"
"You're not upset? We had plans."
"Of course I'll miss you," she said. "But you sound so happy, Bhupen. That's the best part."
The screen went black mid-laugh. She sat on the steps, still smiling, the gamosa folded in her lap. She would post it to Delhi.

qa.q: How far away was Rongali Bihu when Bhupen called?
qa.a: Rongali Bihu was three days away.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel on hearing that Bhupen will miss Bihu week?
qa.a: She is genuinely delighted for him, grinning till her cheeks hurt, while admitting she will miss him.

qa.q: What could Nikita do to stay close while Bhupen is on tour?
qa.a: Post the gamosa to Delhi as she plans, and fix a time to talk so she can hear about the shows.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhupen to hear Nikita's reaction?
qa.a: Bhupen, who worried she would be upset, is likely relieved and feels secure, free to enjoy the tour knowing she is happy for him.

grounding: A young adult is delighted by her boyfriend's selection even though it costs them their festival week together.

subtype: Person whose success is celebrated feels safe [Receiver]
passage: Tarun, you asked why I made such a fuss over your promotion last week. Let me tell you about the Eid week when I was twenty-five. I had just been told I would lead the new app project, and I nearly kept it to myself; in my last office, good news brought only sour faces. But I blurted it to Meher, the senior designer. She jumped up, hugged me across the desk, and next morning brought sheer khurma for the whole floor. "Ojas is leading this one, everyone!" Nobody smirked. I remember my shoulders dropping. After that I pitched ideas I had been sitting on for a year. So when your news came, I knew exactly what to do.

qa.q: What did Meher bring for the whole floor?
qa.a: Sheer khurma, the next morning.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after Meher's reaction, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ojas felt safe and relieved, shoulders dropping, and confident enough to pitch ideas that had been held back for a year.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ojas's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to tell Meher despite the sour faces at the last office; her sincere joy showed Ojas that ambition was welcome there.

qa.q: How might Meher have seen her own celebration?
qa.a: To Meher it was probably simple gladness at a colleague's chance, without knowing how much it would free Ojas to share ideas.

grounding: An elder recalls how a senior's sincere gladness at the speaker's news made ambition feel safe, and passing that generosity on.

subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage:
Diwali vacation, and Himani was stuck at the dental clinic where Mumma worked the front desk. By two o'clock she had read every poster about brushing, twice.
"I'm so bored," she sighed, sliding down the plastic chair.
"Hmm," said Hansa aunty from the second desk, and went back to her files.
Nobody handed her a phone. The fan clicked. A pigeon walked along the window ledge.
Twenty minutes later Himani was on her knees by the umbrella stand, whispering. Each umbrella had a secret owner. The spotty one belonged to a spy. The black one with the broken spoke was a retired pirate's. When a patient came out and picked up the spotty one, Himani gasped. "Mumma! The spy's leaving!"

qa.q: What was walking along the window ledge?
qa.a: A pigeon.

qa.q: How was Himani feeling before the umbrella game began?
qa.a: She felt restless and bored, sighing and sliding down the plastic chair after reading every poster twice.

qa.q: What did the adults do that helped the umbrella game appear?
qa.a: They did not rush to fill the time with a phone or a task, so her boredom had room to turn into imagination.

qa.q: What would change if someone had handed Himani a phone at two o'clock?
qa.a: She would probably have been entertained, but the spy and pirate umbrella game might never have been invented.

grounding: A bored child on a holiday afternoon, left unhurried, invents a game about secret umbrella owners.

subtype: Restless emptiness with nothing to want [Actor]
passage: Looking back, those Christmas holidays in Class 9 were the strangest. I had everything I usually begged for: two weeks off, Zubin and the others texting every hour, a new football game Papa had bought. And I felt nothing. Zubin would message, "Madhav, turf at five?" and I'd type "maybe" and not go. I'd start the game and quit after ten minutes. Even the plum cake Mamma baked tasted like cardboard. It wasn't sadness exactly. It was more like standing in a room where all the lights work but nothing is worth looking at. I kept thinking, what is any of this for? Only later did I see I wasn't tired of games. I was hungry for something that mattered.

qa.q: What did Zubin ask Madhav in the message?
qa.a: "Madhav, turf at five?"

qa.q: How does Madhav describe the feeling during those holidays?
qa.a: Madhav felt flat and empty rather than sad, like standing in a room where all the lights work but nothing is worth looking at.

qa.q: What small step might have helped Madhav at the time?
qa.a: Trying something with a purpose, such as helping a neighbour or learning a skill, and telling Zubin or a parent how flat everything felt.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt getting "maybe" and then no-shows?
qa.a: Zubin may have felt puzzled or a little hurt, not knowing the flatness had nothing to do with the friendship.

grounding: A teenager with friends and games feels flat, finds nothing tempting, and later sees a hunger for meaning underneath.

subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage:
For two years Akash had chased one thing: a seat at the design institute in Ahmedabad. Now it was Navratri, week three of term, the hostel power was out, and garba music thumped up from the lawn below.
Mahima Didi video-called on his last bit of battery. "So? Living the dream?"
"Yeah. It's great," he said, and heard how thin it sounded.
He didn't know how to explain it. No mock tests to plan, no rank to chase, no countdown on the wall. The thing that had pulled him out of bed every morning was simply done. His sketchbook lay open at a blank page.
"You look tired," Mahima said.
"Just the heat," he lied, and watched the dancers circle without wanting to join.

qa.q: How long had Akash chased a seat at the design institute?
qa.a: For two years.

qa.q: Why does Akash's "It's great" sound thin, and what is he feeling?
qa.a: He feels oddly hollow and weary, because the goal that pulled him out of bed each morning is done and nothing has replaced the direction it gave.

qa.q: What could Akash try over the next few weeks?
qa.a: Set a small new aim, like a sketchbook project or a club, and tell Mahima honestly how flat he feels instead of blaming the heat.

qa.q: How might Mahima read Akash's answers on the call?
qa.a: Mahima notices he looks tired and probably senses something off behind "It's great", which may leave her quietly worried.

grounding: A young adult who reached a long-chased college goal feels hollow once the direction it gave is gone.

passage:
In the week before Chhath, the whole of Buxar was sweeping ghats and stringing lights, but Sangeeta's days stayed the same colour. The 8:10 shared auto to the co-operative office. The same ledger, the same stamp, the same three questions from the same farmers. The 5:40 auto home.
She wasn't unhappy, exactly. Just grey, like a shirt washed too many times.
Her cousin Sunaina knocked that evening. "Come and help us paint the ghat steps, na? It'll be fun."
"I'm tired," Sangeeta said, and she was, though she had done nothing heavy.
After Sunaina left, she lay on the cot with her phone, thumb flicking through short videos she would not remember, until the screen said 1:12 a.m.

qa.q: What time was the shared auto to the co-operative office?
qa.a: The 8:10 shared auto.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel about her days, and what does the passage compare it to?
qa.a: She feels grey and tired of the sameness rather than sad, like a shirt washed too many times.

qa.q: What went wrong that evening, and what could change it?
qa.a: She turned down Sunaina and numbed out on videos till after one; saying yes to painting the ghat steps, or any small new activity, could break the grey pattern.

qa.q: What might Sunaina feel after Sangeeta says she's tired?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel disappointed and a little concerned, since painting the steps together was meant to be fun.

grounding: A young professional stuck in the same commute and tasks feels grey and drifts into late-night scrolling instead of change.

subtype: Answering ennui with meaning and, if heavy, with help [Response]
passage:
Thursday, 10:50 pm
Week three of the experiment. Tuesday was the pottery class above the sweet shop; my bowl came out lopsided and I laughed properly for the first time in ages. Sunday I walked dogs at the shelter, and a one-eyed dog called Biscuit refused to leave my side. I've started taking the long route by the lake instead of the flyover. Small things, but the days have edges again.
Still, the mornings are heavy, and it has been like this since before Diwali. Months now. Ira said on the phone tonight, "Sachin, you don't have to wait till it's unbearable." So I did it. Booked a counsellor at the clinic near the office for Saturday, 11 am. Weirdly, I feel lighter already, just writing that down.

qa.q: When is Sachin's appointment with the counsellor?
qa.a: Saturday, 11 am, at the clinic near the office.

qa.q: How does Sachin feel after booking the counsellor?
qa.a: Sachin feels lighter, relieved to have taken a step instead of waiting for the heaviness to lift by itself.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's choices would you advise someone feeling flat to copy?
qa.a: Adding new things such as pottery, dog-walking and a different route, and, since the heavy mornings have lasted months, talking to a counsellor as well.

qa.q: Why might Ira have urged Sachin not to wait?
qa.a: Ira likely felt caring and concerned, seeing the heaviness had gone on for months and believing help is worth getting before things become unbearable.

grounding: An adult fights flatness with new activities and, as the heaviness lasts, books a counsellor instead of waiting it out.

passage:
Lohri week had brought thick fog to Ludhiana, and Mama had gone to Nani's village for four days. At midday recess, while the others chased each other round the swings, Jasleen sat on the bottom step, holding Mama's butterfly hair clip tight in her fist. She didn't cry. She just watched the school gate, where the fog swallowed the road.
Her tiffin stayed shut. When Himani Ma'am sat down beside her and asked, "Missing someone?" Jasleen only nodded and pressed the clip against her cheek.

qa.q: What was Jasleen holding in her fist?
qa.a: Mama's butterfly hair clip.

qa.q: How can you tell Jasleen felt a longing for Mama even though she didn't cry?
qa.a: She went quiet, sat apart watching the gate, left her tiffin shut and pressed the clip to her cheek, all signs of an ache of longing.

qa.q: How could Himani Ma'am support Jasleen for the rest of the day?
qa.a: Stay close, let Jasleen keep the clip, and perhaps help her draw a picture for Mama or count the days until Mama comes back.

qa.q: What might Himani Ma'am notice that the other children miss?
qa.a: That a quiet child with a shut tiffin can be just as sad as one in tears.

grounding: A young child holds a keepsake and quietly watches the school gate at midday, missing her mother.

passage: Pradeep, before you pack for your new school, let me tell you about my first Pongal away. I was thirteen, at a boarding school up in Ooty. Back home they would be boiling the pongal pot over, Amma shouting "Pongalo pongal!", Appa's radio playing nadaswaram from five in the morning. In the dormitory there was only rain on the tin roof and eleven other children breathing. I lay awake with the blanket up to my nose, smelling Amma's ghee in my memory. When my roommate Lalitha asked, "Keerthana, why are your eyes red?" I said it was a cold. I was so afraid of being called a baby. On the third night I told Lalitha the truth. She had been crying into her pillow too.

qa.q: What did Keerthana tell Lalitha about the red eyes?
qa.a: That it was a cold.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana hide the homesickness from Lalitha?
qa.a: Keerthana was afraid of seeming childish, so felt ashamed of missing home food and sounds and pretended to have a cold.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did it change?
qa.a: On the third night Keerthana told Lalitha the truth and learned Lalitha had been crying too, so neither had to hide alone.

qa.q: What might those nights have been like for Lalitha?
qa.a: Lalitha was likely just as homesick and lonely, crying into her pillow while keeping it hidden too.

grounding: An elder recalls lying awake homesick at boarding school and hiding it from a roommate for fear of seeming childish.
